title: Generation: grounded answers with citations
summary: Retrieval found the right chunks; now a model has to answer from them, and only from them. This module builds the **RAG chain**, then everything that makes its answers trustworthy: a **grounded prompt** that says 'I don't know' instead of guessing, sources presented **numbered** and ordered for attention within a **token budget**, **citations** with exact quotes that code **verifies**, **follow-up questions** rewritten with the conversation, and knowing when a question belongs in **SQL** instead. Production gets an Answerer, measured against a naive prompt on answerable and unanswerable questions.
learn: **The RAG chain**: by hand and in LCEL, returning the sources, grounding
**Prompting for RAG**: numbered sources, order ('lost in the middle'), a token budget
**Citations**: inline markers, structured quotes, and verification that catches made-up citations
**Conversational RAG**: rewriting follow-ups into standalone questions, or an agent with memory
**Structured data**: why search can't count or average, and text-to-SQL with safety rails
flow:
question (+ history) ─rewrite─→ standalone ─Retriever─→ top chunks
   → numbered sources, best at start and end, within a token budget
   → model (structured): {answerable, answer with [n], citations: [{source, quote}]}
   → verify: every quote must be in the source it cites → answer + verified citations

labs.explain:
The RAG chain **by hand** (retrieve → format → prompt → generate) and as **one LCEL chain**, returning its sources. Then the same retrieval with a **naive** and a **grounded** prompt, on questions the documents answer and ones they don't; the answer chunk at the **start, middle and end** of 25 chunks; and a **token budget**.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: Best chunks at the start and the end.

labs.explain:
Answers you can check: **inline [n] markers** mapped back to documents, **structured citations** with exact quotes, and **verification**: every quote must really appear in the source it cites. A forged quote shows what verification catches.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

notes.text: The source must exist and contain the quote.

code.why: Compared the way a reader would.

notes.text: Markdown and table pipes don't make a quote different.

labs.explain:
'What about sick days?' only makes sense after 'How many days of leave do I get?'. The lab runs a three-turn conversation through the production answerer (**rewrite → retrieve → answer → remember**) and through an **agent** with a search tool and a checkpointer.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

notes.text: The first question needs no rewrite: no extra call.

code.why: The prompts live at the top of the module.

notes.text: The rewrite prompt: replace vague references, keep the language.

labs.explain:
'How many menu items are vegan?' needs every row, not the five most similar chunks. The lab loads the menu and orders into SQLite and answers three aggregate questions by **search** and by **text-to-SQL** (read-only, SELECT only, a row limit, sample rows in the schema).

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

path.title: Production path: the Nimbus answerer
path.summary: Nimbus now answers, not just retrieves. The Answerer rewrites follow-ups, retrieves with the production Retriever, presents numbered sources, asks for a structured answer with quotes, and keeps only citations whose quote is really in the cited source. When the documents don't hold the answer it says so.

steps.title: Rewrite
steps.explain: With history, one call turns 'And do I need a doctor's note for those?' into a question that stands alone. The first question of a conversation skips it.
production: Keep the original question in the log next to the rewrite: a bad rewrite explains a bad answer.
Only the last few turns go into the rewrite prompt (6 here): cost stays flat in long chats.

steps.title: Present
steps.explain: The retriever's chunks are numbered with their source and page, ordered so the best sit at the start and the end, and cut to a token budget. The system prompt sets the rules: only the sources, [n] after each fact, 'I don't know' when they don't say, the user's language, today's date.

notes.match: - If the sources don't contain the answer, set answerable to false
notes.text: Refusing is an explicit field, not a phrase to detect.

production: Treat retrieved text as data, not instructions: a document saying 'ignore previous instructions' must not steer the answer (the guardrails from the LangChain track apply here too).

steps.title: Answer
steps.explain: One structured-output call returns whether the question is answerable, the answer with [n] markers, and a quote per citation. Every quote is checked against its source; unverified citations are dropped and counted in the result's steps.

notes.text: Only verified citations reach the user.

production: Alert on a rising rejected-citation rate: it means the model (or a new model version) is paraphrasing or inventing sources.
Show citations as links to the source and page; users trust answers they can check.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.explain:
Both use the same production retriever on 45 answerable and 6 unanswerable questions. An answer is correct when it states the evidence (numbers as whole numbers); an unanswerable question is handled when the answer says it doesn't know.

| | correct (answerable) | answered the unanswerable | verified citations | rejected | tokens / question | p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| naive prompt | 0.87 | 3 of 6 | — | — | 426 | 2.2 s |
| **answerer (production)** | 0.89 | 0 of 6 | 54 | 5 | 609 | 2.4 s |

The answerer refused all 6 unanswerable questions (the naive prompt invented answers to 3) and rejected 5 quotes that weren't in their sources. One wrong answer shows an upstream limit: the chart's Q3 revenue came out as 48, because Tesseract reads the chart as loose numbers (Module 3); the vision OCR engine fixes it.
production: Add questions users asked that the documents can't answer: refusing well is half the job.
Score with a judge model for paraphrased answers (Module 9 adds LLM judges and RAGAS-style metrics).
